news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire social care overspent £6.521m in the year; council as a whole underspent by £2.0m
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council's social care services spent £6.521m more than budgeted in the year, but the council as a whole finished £2.0m under budget. Figures in an appendix to the Governance and Audit Committee's papers for 6 October show the overspend was offset by underspends elsewhere.

Children's Services accounts for most of it, with an overspend of £5.649m. Adult Services overspent by £0.872m. Together they make up the £6.521m. The appendix sets out the position in the council's outturn (the actual figures for the year once it has ended, as against what was budgeted).

Other services spent less than planned and covered the gap. Infrastructure underspent by £1.977m, and Education also finished under budget. The net result across the council was the £2.0m underspend. The figures in the appendix are the council's own and are presented by service, with no explanation of the causes of the social care overspends.

news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire puts 92% of second homes council tax premium into its budget, with a £23.3m gap for 2027-28
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council puts 92% of the money raised from its council tax premium on second homes into its general budget, Cabinet papers for 5 October show. The premium is the extra charge the council applies on top of standard council tax for second homes. In 2026-27, £9.008m of it goes to general fund services, the council's main day-to-day spending account.

The money pays for core services, including homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m) and public realm maintenance. The paper says the premium therefore covers parts of those services that would otherwise have to be paid for from other sources of day-to-day spending.

That matters because the council projects a funding gap of £23.3m for 2027-28, the shortfall between what it expects to spend and what it expects to have. The council's Director of Resources sets out what changing the premium would do to that gap. The paper says: "Based on the current allocation of 92% of the second homes Council Tax premium income to the Council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities, a 25% decrease in the premium would increase the funding gap for 2027-28 by circa. £1.4m". A 25% change in the premium level would move the gap by about £1.4m either way.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: West Wales region continuing to experience high levels of delayed hospital discharges affecting emergency care capacity
findings.detail: A multi-council performance audit review identified ongoing challenges in supporting timely discharge from hospital across Pembrokeshire, Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion and Hywel Dda Health Board. Audit Wales issued 15 recommendations on capacity, discharge planning, information sharing, policy development and scrutiny arrangements to support regional improvement.
findings.matters: Delayed hospital discharge typically reflects adult social care capacity constraints; this can drive future service cost pressures and demand volatility, affecting council financial planning and resilience.
findings.figures: 15 recommendations across four partner organisations; 4-council regional review
findings.quote: High levels of delayed discharges continue to impact urgent and emergency care services.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Council has significantly strengthened corporate risk management arrangements in recent years
findings.detail: Audit Wales found the council operates within an up-to-date risk management framework supported by a positive risk management culture. Four recommendations were made for further enhancement in risk appetite and tolerance, escalation and de-escalation criteria, and risk reporting.
findings.matters: Robust risk management is foundational to council financial resilience; strong governance frameworks support a lender's confidence in the council's ability to navigate financial pressures.
findings.figures: Four recommendations identified for further enhancement
findings.quote: Audit Wales found that the Council has significantly strengthened its risk management arrangements in recent years and now operates within an up-to-date framework supported by a positive risk management culture.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Audit identified improvements needed in capital accounting processes before final sign-off
findings.detail: Audit Wales identified issues in capital transactions and balances that were corrected before final accounts approval. Recommendations were made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.
findings.matters: Capital is typically material on local authority balance sheets; control weaknesses in capital accounting raise questions about the strength of underlying accounting control frameworks.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not disclosed; issues corrected before approval
findings.quote: Recommendations have been made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Draft 2024-25 accounts delivered after statutory deadline but received unqualified audit opinion with no material misstatements
findings.detail: Audit Wales received the council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Improvements were needed in capital accounting, but these were corrected. Subject to council approval, an unqualified opinion is intended, with audit completion scheduled for 16 October 2026.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence both in the reliability of financial statements and in the council's ability to meet financial governance timelines; late submission signals a process control issue.
findings.figures: Accounts delivered 12 November 2025, audit completion 16 October 2026
findings.quote: Audit Wales received the Council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Whilst improvements were required in relation to capital transactions and balances, the accounts were found to be properly prepared and materially accurate, with no uncorrected misstatements.

findings.headline: Compressed timetable for 2025-26 and 2026-27 audits requires completion of two audit cycles within ten months; draft 2025-26 accounts due 23 November 2026
findings.detail: To recover from 2024-25 delays and meet statutory deadlines, the council must submit draft 2025-26 accounts by 23 November 2026 and receive audit completion by 31 March 2027 at latest. This allows preparation of 2026-27 accounts by the 30 June 2027 deadline. The auditor explicitly describes this as 'a challenging timetable' and notes success depends on consistent delivery of high-quality statements and working papers.
findings.matters: This signals whether the council has resolved the underlying capacity and process issues that caused 2024-25 problems. Success is uncertain—the auditor states the timetable is challenging. Failure to meet 2025-26 deadlines would trigger further delays, renewed governance concerns, and potential need to disclose financial control deficiencies.
findings.figures: 23 November 2026 draft submission target; 31 March 2027 audit completion target; two audit cycles in ten months
findings.quote: This is a challenging timetable, as two audit cycles will need to be completed within 10 months.
